©Idaho State University, 2022 SCOPE AND CONTENT NOTE The Edward Stevenson Research Collection consists of documents, correspondence, photographs, newspaper clippings, tapes, and personal items about Edward Stevenson and Daniel Alkofer’s research project on him. Edward Stevenson was a costume and fashion designer from the 1920s through the 1960s. He was born in Pocatello, Idaho but as a child, he and his mother moved to California where his career started. He worked for RKO for most of his career and helmed the costume department at RKO, designing for such films as Love Affair with Irene Dunne, Citizen Kane, The Magnificent Ambersons, It’s a Wonderful Life and Cheaper by the Dozen. Towards the end of his career, Stevenson designed Lucille Ball’s costumes for her projects such as The Facts of Life and the I Love Lucy television series. ARRANGEMENT The Collection is arranged in seven (7) series, and although it does not retain its original order, the folder information and descriptions remain intact. Series I, BIOGRAPHY, contains Alkofer’s credentials; Series II, CORRESPONDENCE, contains correspondence between Alkofer and Malcom Mayers, and others he was in contact with in regard to his research on Stevenson; Series III contains Alkofer’s RESEARCH notes about Edward Stevenson’s life including his works, his coworkers, his friends, and his family; Series IV contains Alkofer’s WRITINGS about Edward Stevenson’s life; Series V contains newspaper clippings from Pocatello newspapers about Stevenson’s work with POCATELLO HIGH SCHOOL; Series VI contains PHOTOGRAPHS of Edward Stevenson’s work and of his family; Series VII contains AUDIO CASSETTE TAPES of interviews that Alkofer recorded for his research.

# Page 3^page=3
©Idaho State University, 2022 BIOGRAPHICAL NOTE Written by Trent Clegg, Graduate Assistant, 2007 Edward Manson Stevenson was born in Pocatello, Idaho at his family’s residence on the 13th of May 1906 to Mr. Andrew B. Stevenson (1865 –1919), then superintendent of the Idaho Division of the Oregon Shortline Railroad, and Mrs. Jennie Dolly Uhland Stevenson (d. 1951). He attended the St. Joseph School and Pocatello High School, until 1922, when, at the age of sixteen, he moved permanently to California, where he finished his schooling at Hollywood High School. While still in school, his neighbor, Lova Klenowsky became aware of his artistic abilities and introduced him to André Andreive (1886 –1966) world-famous fashion designer, who took Stevenson on as an apprentice. Stevenson’s first job in the industry was as a sketch artist for Norma Talmadge Productions, rendering the design ideas of others. He was also allowed to create designs of his own, some of which were included in the company’s productions of the time, most notably a silver gown worn in The White Moth by Barbara La Marr. The next year, 1925, Stevenson worked as a sketch artist for André-Ani at MGM, designing for Greta Garbo. Finally, in 1928, through the influence of another Fox actress, Louise Fazenda, Stevenson landed his first big contract as a designer with First National Pictures, quickly becoming the head of the department. Between 1931 and 1935, Stevenson found work in a variety of ways and places. The Pocatello Tribune reported on November 11, 1931 that Stevenson “joined the Blakely House Company” where he “designed gowns for Constance Bennett, Jean Harlow, Mrs. Lawrence Tibbett and other notables.” He designed for Thelma Todd at Hal Roach Studios and Barbara Stanwyck at Columbia Pictures, among others. He also set up his own shop, Blakely House, which designed clothes for the stars and those who admired them. In 1935, Stevenson started working as assistant to Bernard Newman at RKO. From late 1936 until 1949 when his contract expired, Stevenson helmed the costume department at RKO, designing for such films as Gunga Din, Love Affair with Irene Dunne, Citizen Kane, The Magnificent Ambersons, Sinbad the Sailor, The Bachelor and the Bobby Soxer, It’s a Wonderful Life, Cheaper by the Dozen, and The Mudlark. He continued to work for RKO occasionally until 1956. In 1955, Lucille Ball, a former ‘B’ movie actress who had worked with Stevenson in the heyday of RKO and now was revolutionizing the infant world of television with her sitcom, I Love Lucy, called him back to work. From that point until the end of his life, the designer worked for “The First Lady of Television”, exclusively so from 1960 onward. It was his work on a Lucille Ball film, The Facts of Life (1960), that Stevenson won his solitary Academy Award for Black and White Costume Design, in tandem with his colleague and competitor, Edith Head. Television was an enjoyable challenge for Stevens on and he did some of his most imaginative work during this period. Chierichetti notes that the Ball years saw Stevenson designing “high

# Page 4^page=4
©Idaho State University, 2022 fashions, period costumes, and clothes that would hide props for Lucy and her many guest stars.” In the I Love Lucy episode, “Lucy Does a Tango”, Stevenson designed a costume with pockets in which Lucy hid eggs. When Desi pulled Lucy close for the tango, the eggs were discovered. This was one of Stevenson’s favorite assignments. Ms. Ball reciprocated ‘Eddie’s’ devotion until the day he died of a coronary on 2 December 1968, fittingly, while shopping for fabric on La Cienega Bioulevard in Los Angeles. Edward Stevenson is buried in the Mountainview Cemetery in Pocatello, though the location of his grave is obscured by the fact that his headstone rests on what, according to cemetery records, should be the grave of his sister-in-law.

Stevenson born, Pocatello, Idaho, May 13 1922 Stevenson and his mother move permanently to California 1925 Stevenson worked as a sketch artist for André-Ani at MGM Studios 1928 Joined First National Pictures and quickly became head of the design department 1930 First National Pictures purchased by Warner Brothers 1931 Stevenson’s contract with Warner Brothers expired 1931-1935 Stevenson worked independently, setting up his own shop and designing for studios lacking their own wardrobe department. 1935 Started working as an assistant to Bernard Newman at RKO 1936-1949 Head of Costume Department for RKO 1950 Oscar nomination for The Mudlark and David and Bathsheba 1950-1956 Continued working occasionally for RKO 1955 Started Working for Lucille Ball 1960 Began working exclusively for Lucille Ball won an Oscar for The Facts of Life 1968 Edward Stevenson died, Los Angeles, California, December 2
